sections.heading: 6.1 What comes next?
sections.excerpt: Each new square adds 3 matches, so 4 squares use 13. Keep adding 3: 16, 19, 22, 25, 28 and 31. A row of 10 squares uses 31 matches.

steps.text: Kym makes a row of squares from matchsticks. 1 square uses 4 matches, 2 squares use 7 and 3 squares use 10. How many matches do 4 squares use? And 10 squares?
Each new square adds 3 matches, so 4 squares use 13. Keep adding 3: 16, 19, 22, 25, 28 and 31. A row of 10 squares uses 31 matches.
Draw the rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4 squares, one under another. Write the count of matches beside each row: 4, 7, 10, 13. Between each pair of counts, write + 3.
Why 3 and not 4? The first square needs 4 matches. Each square after it borrows its left side from the square before, so it needs only 3 new matches.

A list of numbers made by a rule is called a sequence. Each number in it is a term. A rule that makes each term from the one before, like "add 3", is a term-to-term rule. The first term and the term-to-term rule fix every term after them.
Start at 2 and double each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The term-to-term rule is "multiply by 2". Start at 50 and take away 6 each time: 50, 44, 38, 32. The rule there is "subtract 6".
The tempting slip is to say 10 squares need 10 × 4 = 40 matches. That counts each shared side twice. A row of 10 squares has 9 shared sides, and 40 − 9 = 31.
A sequence starts 3, 10, 17, 24. What is the next term?
A sequence follows a rule, and a term-to-term rule makes each term from the one before.

sections.heading: 6.2 Equal steps
sections.excerpt: Take each term away from the next one. For the first list the gaps are 4, 4, 4 and 4. For the second they are 2, 4, 8 and 16. Only the first list grows in equal steps.

steps.text: Look at 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 and at 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Both lists grow. Which one grows by the same amount every time?
Take each term away from the next one. For the first list the gaps are 4, 4, 4 and 4. For the second they are 2, 4, 8 and 16. Only the first list grows in equal steps.
Draw each list as a row of columns, as tall as its terms. The first row climbs like a staircase with every step 4 high. The second row's steps keep doubling.
Why look at the gaps? Equal gaps mean the term-to-term rule is "add the same number". Then you can jump ahead without listing every term, as the next section shows.

When the gap between neighbouring terms is always the same, that gap is the common difference. A sequence with a common difference is an arithmetic sequence. A sequence that multiplies by the same number each time, like 2, 4, 8, 16, is a geometric sequence.
In 7, 4, 1, −2, −5 each term is 3 less than the one before. So it is an arithmetic sequence with common difference −3, and its next term is −8.
One slip is to give the common difference of 40, 35, 30 as 5. The terms go down, and 35 − 40 = −5. Another slip is to call 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic. Its gaps are 3, 5 and 7, which are not equal.
What is the common difference of 11, 8, 5, 2?
An arithmetic sequence goes up or down by its common difference every time.

sections.heading: 6.3 Jumping to any term
sections.excerpt: The counts go up by 3, like the 3 times table: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each count is 1 more than that: 4, 7, 10, 13. So 100 squares use 3 × 100 + 1 = 301 matches.

steps.text: The matchstick rows used 4, 7, 10 and 13 matches. How many matches does a row of 100 squares use, without listing 100 terms?
The counts go up by 3, like the 3 times table: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each count is 1 more than that: 4, 7, 10, 13. So 100 squares use 3 × 100 + 1 = 301 matches.
Make a table with three rows. The top row is the position: 1, 2, 3, 4. The middle row is 3 times the position: 3, 6, 9, 12. The bottom row is the matches: 4, 7, 10, 13.
Why 3 times the position? Every square adds 3 matches, so n squares add up to 3n of them. The + 1 is the single match on the far left that starts the row.

A rule that gives a term from its position n is called the nth term, or the position-to-term rule. For the matchsticks it is 3n + 1. In an arithmetic sequence, the number in front of n is the common difference.
Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14. The common difference is 3, so start from 3n: 3, 6, 9, 12. Each term is 2 more, so the nth term is 3n + 2. The 20th term is 3 × 20 + 2 = 62.

The tempting slip is to write n + 3, because the terms go up by 3. That gives 4, 5, 6, 7. Another slip is to add the first term, as in 3n + 5, which starts at 8. Test n = 1 and n = 2 before you trust a rule.
Find the nth term of 9, 14, 19, 24.
Start the nth term from the common difference times n, then fix it so the first term is right.

sections.heading: 6.4 Is it in the list?
sections.excerpt: The rows have 12, 15, 18, … seats. They go up by 3, so start from 3n: 3, 6, 9. Each row has 9 more than that, so row n has 3n + 9. For 57 seats, 3n + 9 = 57, so 3n = 48 and n = 16. For 50 seats, 3n = 41 and n = 13⅔.

steps.text: In a hall, row 1 has 12 seats and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front. Which row has 57 seats? Does any row have exactly 50?

The rows have 12, 15, 18, … seats. They go up by 3, so start from 3n: 3, 6, 9. Each row has 9 more than that, so row n has 3n + 9. For 57 seats, 3n + 9 = 57, so 3n = 48 and n = 16. For 50 seats, 3n = 41 and n = 13⅔.
Draw a number line and mark the seat counts 12, 15, 18 and on up to 57. The number 50 falls between 48 and 51, which are rows 13 and 14.
Why does 13⅔ mean no? Positions count rows: the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd. There is no row 13⅔, so no row has exactly 50 seats.
To test whether a number is a term, set the nth term equal to it and solve the equation. A whole number answer is its position. Any other answer means it is not a term.
Is 99 a term of 7n − 6? Solve 7n − 6 = 99. Then 7n = 105, so n = 15. Yes, 99 is the 15th term. Check: 7 × 15 − 6 = 99.
The tempting slip is to put 50 in place of n: 3 × 50 + 9 = 159. That finds how many seats row 50 has. It does not find which row has 50 seats.
Which term of 5n − 2 is 83?
Set the nth term equal to the number and solve. A whole number answer is its position.

sections.heading: 6.5 When the steps grow
sections.excerpt: The gaps 3, 5 and 7 are the first differences. Find the gaps between them: 5 − 3 = 2 and 7 − 5 = 2. Those are equal. The tile counts are 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 4 × 4, so the nth one is n².

steps.text: Kym builds squares of tiles: 1 tile, then 4, then 9, then 16. The gaps are 3, 5 and 7, so they are not equal. Is there still a rule?
The gaps 3, 5 and 7 are the first differences. Find the gaps between them: 5 − 3 = 2 and 7 − 5 = 2. Those are equal. The tile counts are 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 4 × 4, so the nth one is n².
Draw the squares of 1, 4 and 9 tiles inside one another. Each new square adds an L-shaped border of 3, then 5, then 7 tiles.
Why does each border grow by 2? A 3 by 3 square becomes 4 by 4 when you add a row of 3, a column of 3 and 1 corner. From n by n, the border is n + n + 1 = 2n + 1 tiles, which goes up by 2 each time.

The gaps between the first differences are the second differences. When the second differences are equal, and not 0, the list is a quadratic sequence. Its nth term has an n², and the number in front of n² is half the second difference.

Take 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. The first differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, and the second differences are all 2, so start from n². Take away 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 to leave 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which is n. So the nth term is n² + n.
The usual slip is to put the second difference itself in front of n². With a second difference of 2, the rule 2n² gives 2, 8, 18, not 1, 4, 9. Halve the second difference first.
Find the nth term of 4, 7, 12, 19, 28.
Equal second differences mean a quadratic sequence, with half the second difference in front of n².

sections.heading: 6.6 Adding up a staircase
sections.excerpt: Try 1 to 10 first. Pair the first number with the last: 1 + 10 = 11, then 2 + 9 = 11, and so on. There are 5 pairs of 11, which make 55. From 1 to 100 there are 50 pairs of 101, which make 5050.

steps.text: A teacher once asked a class to add every whole number from 1 to 100. A boy called Gauss gave the answer in about a minute. How could he be so quick?
Try 1 to 10 first. Pair the first number with the last: 1 + 10 = 11, then 2 + 9 = 11, and so on. There are 5 pairs of 11, which make 55. From 1 to 100 there are 50 pairs of 101, which make 5050.
In the figure, set the terms to 5, the first term to 1 and the common difference to 1. The red staircase 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the blue copy above it make a rectangle 5 wide and 6 high.
Why is every column the same height? Moving right, the red step rises by 1 and the blue step falls by 1. So each column stays 6 high, the rectangle holds 30 squares, and one staircase holds 15.

The totals 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 of 1 + 2 + … + n are the triangular numbers, and the nth one is n(n + 1) ÷ 2. The same pairing adds any arithmetic sequence. Multiply the number of terms by the first term plus the last, then halve.
Add 2 + 5 + 8 + … + 29. The nth term is 3n − 1, and 3n − 1 = 29 gives n = 10, so there are 10 terms. The sum is 10 × (2 + 29) ÷ 2 = 155.
The tempting slip is to forget the halving and say 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 100 × 101 = 10,100. The rectangle holds two staircases, so that counts every number twice.
To add equal steps, multiply the number of terms by the first term plus the last, and halve.

debate.title: Twice as many squares
debate.contextPrompt: A row of 10 matchstick squares uses 31 matches, and the nth term is 3n + 1. Ishaan and Tara work out the matches for a row of 20 squares.
debate.speakerAClaim: 20 squares is twice 10 squares, so it needs twice 31. That is 62 matches.
debate.speakerBClaim: Put n = 20 in the nth term. 3 × 20 + 1 = 61 matches.

choices.reasoningStatement: Twice the squares always needs twice the matches.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Put two rows of 10 squares end to end. Where they meet, two matches stand side by side. Do you need both of them?

choices.reasoningStatement: The nth term gives any term from its position.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Doubling 3n + 1 gives 6n + 2, which counts the starting match twice. The real rule adds that match only once.

choices.reasoningStatement: Each square has 4 sides, and 20 × 4 = 80.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Count the matches in a row of 2 squares. Is it 8, or does one side belong to both?

debate.invariantTakeaway: An nth term like 3n + 1 does not double when n doubles. Find any term by putting its position into the rule.

sections.heading: 7.1 Machines that follow a rule
sections.excerpt: Each extra 1 going in adds 2 coming out, so the machine doubles. 4 doubled is 8, and 11 is 3 more, so it doubles, then adds 3. To get back from 31, take 3 to get 28, then halve to get 14.

steps.text: Kym feeds 4 into a number machine and 11 comes out. Feeding in 5 gives 13, and 10 gives 23. What does the machine do? What went in if 31 came out?
Each extra 1 going in adds 2 coming out, so the machine doubles. 4 doubled is 8, and 11 is 3 more, so it doubles, then adds 3. To get back from 31, take 3 to get 28, then halve to get 14.
Draw two boxes in a row: in, then × 2, then + 3, then out. Under them, draw the same two boxes with the arrows pointing back: − 3, then ÷ 2.
Why undo the steps in reverse order? The + 3 happened last, so it is the first thing to take off, the way you take off your shoes before your socks.

A rule that turns each input into exactly one output is called a function. A row of boxes showing its steps is a function machine, and we write the rule as f(x) = 2x + 3. Run backwards, each step undone in reverse order, it is the inverse function, f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3) ÷ 2. Say f⁻¹ as "f inverse". The small −1 is a label here, not a power.
Take f(x) = 5x − 4. Then f(3) = 5 × 3 − 4 = 11. The inverse adds 4, then divides by 5, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 4) ÷ 5, and f⁻¹(11) = 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
The tempting slip is to undo the steps in the same order: halve first, then take 3. For 31 that gives 15.5 − 3 = 12.5, and 2 × 12.5 + 3 = 28, not 31.
f(x) = 3x − 7. What is f⁻¹(8)?
A function machine follows its steps in order, and its inverse undoes them in reverse order.

sections.heading: 7.2 Points on a grid
sections.excerpt: The fares are 50, 70, 90, 110 and 130. For each pair, go across by the kilometres and up by the fare, and put a dot. Each dot is 1 across and 20 up from the one before, so the dots sit in a straight row.

steps.text: The taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for each kilometre. Make a table of the fares for 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 km. Then mark each pair of numbers as a dot on squared paper. What shape do the dots make?

The fares are 50, 70, 90, 110 and 130. For each pair, go across by the kilometres and up by the fare, and put a dot. Each dot is 1 across and 20 up from the one before, so the dots sit in a straight row.

Draw a line across the page for the kilometres, 0 to 4, and a line up the side for the fare, 0 to 140 in steps of 20. Put dots at 0 and 50, 1 and 70, 2 and 90, 3 and 110, and 4 and 130, then lay a ruler along them.
Why a straight row? Each extra kilometre adds the same ₹20. Equal steps across give equal steps up, like the arithmetic sequences of chapter 6.

The line across is the x-axis and the line up is the y-axis. They meet at the origin, (0, 0). A point is named by its coordinates (x, y): how far across, then how far up. The taxi's dots are (0, 50), (1, 70), (2, 90), (3, 110) and (4, 130).
The point (3, −2) is 3 to the right of the origin and 2 down. The point (−4, 1) is 4 to the left and 1 up. The x-coordinate always comes first.
The tempting slip is to swap the numbers and put (2, 5) at 2 up and 5 across. Across comes first, in the same way that x comes before y in the alphabet.
Another taxi charges ₹30 to start and ₹15 for each kilometre. What is the y-coordinate of its point for 4 km?
Coordinates (x, y) say how far across, then how far up.

sections.heading: 7.3 How steep?
sections.excerpt: The first row goes up 20 for each 1 across. The second goes up 30 for each 1 across. So the second is steeper: it climbs ₹30 for every kilometre instead of ₹20.

steps.text: For 0, 1 and 2 km, one taxi's fares are 50, 70 and 90, and another's are 50, 80 and 110. Draw both rows of dots. Which row is steeper, and by how much?
The first row goes up 20 for each 1 across. The second goes up 30 for each 1 across. So the second is steeper: it climbs ₹30 for every kilometre instead of ₹20.
On the first row, draw a step from (1, 70) to (3, 110): 2 across, then 40 up. The step and the line make a right-angled triangle.
Why divide the rise by the run? A wider step has a bigger rise as well. 40 up for 2 across is as steep as 20 up for 1 across, and dividing gives 20 both times.
Divide the rise by the run to get the gradient of the line. Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. A line that goes down from left to right has a negative gradient.
Between (−2, 1) and (4, 13), the change in y is 13 − 1 = 12 and the change in x is 4 − (−2) = 6. The gradient is 12 ÷ 6 = 2.

The tempting slip is to divide the run by the rise: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5. Another is to subtract the y values one way round and the x values the other way, which flips the sign. Start from the same point both times.
What is the gradient of the line through (1, 9) and (4, 3)?
The gradient is the rise divided by the run, and it is negative when the line goes down.

sections.heading: 7.4 Reading a line's equation
sections.excerpt: The fare is y = 20x + 50. At x = 0 it is 50, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 50). It climbs 20 for each kilometre, so its gradient is 20. Both numbers sit in the rule.

steps.text: The taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 a kilometre. Write the fare y for x kilometres. Where does its line cross the y-axis, and what is its gradient?
The fare is y = 20x + 50. At x = 0 it is 50, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 50). It climbs 20 for each kilometre, so its gradient is 20. Both numbers sit in the rule.
In the figure, set the gradient to 2, where the line crosses the y-axis to 1 and the step across to 1. The green dot is at (0, 1), and the step goes 1 across and 2 up.
Why is the number in front of x the gradient? Each time x goes up by 1, y goes up by that number. The number on its own is the value of y when x is 0, which is where the line meets the y-axis.

Any rule y = mx + c draws a straight line, called a straight-line graph or a linear graph. m is its gradient. The point (0, c), where it crosses the y-axis, is the y-intercept. The point where it crosses the x-axis, where y = 0, is the x-intercept.
y = 2x + 5 has gradient 2 and y-intercept (0, 5). For the x-intercept, set y = 0. Then 2x + 5 = 0, so 2x = −5 and x = −2.5. The line crosses the x-axis at (−2.5, 0).
The tempting slip is to read the gradient of y = 7 − 3x as 7, because it comes first. Write it as y = −3x + 7. The gradient is −3 and the y-intercept is (0, 7).
Where does y = 4x − 12 cross the x-axis? Give the value of x.
In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is where the line crosses the y-axis.

sections.heading: 7.5 Lines that never meet
sections.excerpt: At every distance the second fare is ₹30 more: 80 against 50, 100 against 70, 120 against 90. The gap never closes, so the lines never meet.

steps.text: Two taxi firms both charge ₹20 a kilometre. One charges ₹50 to start and the other ₹80. Draw both lines. Will they ever meet?
At every distance the second fare is ₹30 more: 80 against 50, 100 against 70, 120 against 90. The gap never closes, so the lines never meet.
Draw y = 20x + 50 and y = 20x + 80 on the same axes. The second line is the first one slid 30 straight up.
Why do they never meet? Both climb 20 for each 1 across, so the gap between them stays 30 however far you go.

Lines that never meet are parallel lines. Two straight lines are parallel when they have the same gradient. Lines that cross at a right angle are perpendicular, and multiplying their gradients gives −1. For example, y = 2x and y = −½x cross at a right angle, and 2 × −½ = −1.
Find the line parallel to y = 3x − 1 through (2, 11). It has gradient 3, so it is y = 3x + c. Put in x = 2 and y = 11: 11 = 6 + c, so c = 5. The line is y = 3x + 5.
The tempting slip is to think y = 2x + 1 and y = x + 2 are parallel because they use the same numbers. Their gradients are 2 and 1, so they cross, at (1, 3).
Which line is parallel to y = 5x + 2: y = 2x + 5, y = 5x − 3 or y = −5x + 2?
Parallel lines have the same gradient and cross the y-axis at different places.

sections.heading: 7.6 The story of a journey
sections.excerpt: Going, Kym covers 12 km in 1 hour, which is 12 km an hour. Coming home, 12 km takes 2 hours, which is 6 km an hour. During the visit, time passes but the distance stays 12 km.

steps.text: Kym cycles 12 km to a friend's house in 1 hour, stays for 1 hour, then rides home in 2 hours. Mark the distance from home against the time. Which part of the trip was fastest?
Going, Kym covers 12 km in 1 hour, which is 12 km an hour. Coming home, 12 km takes 2 hours, which is 6 km an hour. During the visit, time passes but the distance stays 12 km.
Put the time in hours along the x-axis, 0 to 4, and the distance from home up the y-axis, 0 to 12 km. Join (0, 0) to (1, 12), then (1, 12) to (2, 12), then (2, 12) to (4, 0).
Why is the steepest part the fastest? Its gradient is distance ÷ time, which is the speed. The flat part has gradient 0, so Kym is not moving.
A graph of a real situation, like a taxi fare or a trip, is a real-life graph. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and a line sloping down means heading back towards the start.
A bus goes 30 km in the first half hour, then 30 km in the next hour. Its speeds are 30 ÷ 0.5 = 60 km an hour, then 30 ÷ 1 = 30 km an hour. The first part of its line is twice as steep.
The tempting slip is to read the line going down as Kym riding downhill. It shows the distance from home shrinking, so Kym is riding home.
On a distance-time graph, a runner's line goes from (0, 0) to (2, 18), with time in hours and distance in km. What is the runner's speed in km an hour?
On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and a flat line means standing still.

debate.title: Which number is the gradient?
debate.contextPrompt: Arjun and Zara look at the line y = 6 − 2x and argue about its gradient.
debate.speakerAClaim: The gradient is the first number, so it is 6.
debate.speakerBClaim: The gradient is the number in front of x, so it is −2.

choices.reasoningStatement: The gradient is always the first number in the equation.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Work out y when x = 0 and when x = 1. How much did y change for that one step across?

choices.reasoningStatement: The gradient is the number multiplying x, sign and all.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Written as y = −2x + 6, the line falls 2 for every 1 across, and it crosses the y-axis at (0, 6).

choices.reasoningStatement: Steepness is a size, so it cannot be negative.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Is y going up or down as x goes up? What sign tells you which way the line slopes?

debate.invariantTakeaway: The gradient is the number multiplying x, with its sign. Rewrite the rule as y = mx + c before you read it.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Two circles in a class of 30
atlasLessons.question: Why do 18 cricket players and 15 football players make only 26 students who play a sport?
atlasLessons.explanation: The 7 who play both are inside both counts. Take them away once: 18 + 15 − 7 = 26.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Outside both circles
atlasLessons.question: How many of the 30 students play neither sport?
atlasLessons.explanation: 26 play at least one sport, so 30 − 26 = 4 are outside both circles. They make up the complement of A ∪ B.
atlasLessons.limits: The count: n((A ∪ B)′) = 30 − 26 = 4
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Not this and not that
atlasLessons.question: Why is outside A ∪ B the same as outside A and outside B?
atlasLessons.explanation: To be outside the union, a student must miss both sports. Missing one is not enough. So (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.
atlasLessons.limits: De Morgan's law: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Turning round on the number line
atlasLessons.question: What does multiplying by −1 do to a number?
atlasLessons.explanation: It keeps the size and turns the direction round. 3 becomes −3, and −3 becomes 3.
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · What two numbers share
atlasLessons.question: How do the HCF and the LCM of 24 and 36 come from their prime factors?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
atlasLessons.limits: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Why the check always works
atlasLessons.question: Why does HCF × LCM equal the two numbers multiplied together?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 × 36 uses every prime of both numbers. The LCM takes each prime the most times it appears in either number. The HCF takes the shared ones, which are exactly the primes the LCM left out. Between them they use every prime once.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: HCF × LCM = a × b
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · Lining up the repeating digits
atlasLessons.question: Why does multiplying 0.3636… by 100 help to turn it into a fraction?
atlasLessons.explanation: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left. The digits after the point still read 3636…, as they did before. Subtracting the original number removes them all and leaves the whole number 36.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 99 × the number = 36, so the number is 4/11
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · How many pieces fit?
atlasLessons.question: Why is dividing by 2/3 the same as multiplying by 3/2?
atlasLessons.explanation: Cutting each whole into thirds multiplies the count by 3. Grouping the thirds in twos divides it by 2. Doing both is multiplying by 3/2.
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · The decimal that is secretly 1
atlasLessons.question: What fraction is 0.999…?
atlasLessons.explanation: Ten lots of it are 9.999…, and one lot is 0.999…, with the same tail. Take one lot from ten lots and nine lots are exactly 9. So the number is 9/9, which is 1. 0.999… and 1 are two names for one number.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 0.999… = 1
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · Sharing in a ratio
atlasLessons.question: Why do you add the parts of a ratio before you share?
atlasLessons.explanation: The amount is cut into equal parts, and the ratio says how many parts each person takes. Adding tells you how many parts there are in all. Dividing by that number gives the size of one part.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: 1 part = total ÷ number of parts
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · Up 20%, then down 20%
atlasLessons.question: Why does a 20% rise followed by a 20% fall leave you with less?
atlasLessons.explanation: The rise multiplies by 1.2 and the fall multiplies by 0.8. Together they multiply by 0.96. The fall is 20% of the bigger amount, so it takes off more than the rise put on.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · The doubling rule
atlasLessons.question: Why does money at 8% a year double in about 9 years?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each year multiplies the money by 1.08. Nine of those multiplications come to almost exactly 2. The rule of 72 finds the 9 without the long sum: 72 ÷ 8 = 9.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 1.08 multiplied nine times is about 2
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · Multiplying out a bracket
atlasLessons.question: Why does the number outside a bracket multiply every term inside?
atlasLessons.explanation: A bracket is one amount, so 4(x + 3) means four lots of x + 3. Four lots hold four x's and four 3s, which is 4x + 12.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a(b + c) = ab + ac
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · Two brackets
atlasLessons.question: Why does (x + 3)(x + 2) have four pieces?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each bracket is one side of a rectangle, cut into two lengths. Two lengths along the top and two down the side make four pieces. They are x², 3x, 2x and 6, and the two strips join to make 5x.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · The corner cut away
atlasLessons.question: Why is 53² − 47² the same as 6 × 100?
atlasLessons.explanation: Cut a 47 by 47 square from the corner of a 53 by 53 square. The L-shape left over rearranges into a rectangle 6 wide and 100 long.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · The same to both sides
atlasLessons.question: Why does doing the same thing to both sides keep an equation true?
atlasLessons.explanation: An equation says two amounts are equal, like the two pans of a level balance. Change both by the same amount, and they are still equal. Change one only, and the balance tips.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: ax + b = c gives x = (c − b) ÷ a
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · Turning a formula round
atlasLessons.question: Why do you undo the steps of a formula in reverse order?
atlasLessons.explanation: A formula builds its subject in steps, such as × 12 and then + 50. The last step done sits on the outside, so it comes off first.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: C = 50 + 12d gives d = (C − 50) ÷ 12
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · When the sign turns round
atlasLessons.question: Why does dividing by a negative number turn an inequality round?
atlasLessons.explanation: Multiplying by −1 reflects every number across 0. The number that was further right lands further left, so the bigger one becomes the smaller one.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: if a < b, then −a > −b
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Equal steps
atlasLessons.question: How can you tell whether a list of numbers goes up in equal steps?
atlasLessons.explanation: Take each term away from the next one. If every gap is the same, the list is an arithmetic sequence and that gap is its common difference.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: equal gaps d give the nth term dn + c
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Jumping to the 100th term
atlasLessons.question: Why does the number in front of n match the gap between terms?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each step along the list adds the same gap d. After n steps, the gaps add up to dn, and a fixed number corrects the start.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Two staircases make a rectangle
atlasLessons.question: Why is 1 + 2 + … + n half of n × (n + 1)?
atlasLessons.explanation: Turn a copy of the staircase upside down and set it on top. Every column then reaches n + 1, so the two staircases fill a rectangle n by n + 1.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) ÷ 2
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Rise over run
atlasLessons.question: Why does the gradient of a straight line not depend on where you measure it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Any step under a straight line makes a triangle of the same shape. A step twice as wide rises twice as far, so the rise divided by the run never changes.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: gradient = change in y ÷ change in x
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Reading y = mx + c
atlasLessons.question: How can you see a line's steepness and its starting point in its equation?
atlasLessons.explanation: Put x = 0 and y is c, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, c). Each step of 1 across adds m to y, so m is the gradient.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: y = mx + c
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Speed is a gradient
atlasLessons.question: On a distance-time graph, why does a steeper line mean a faster trip?
atlasLessons.explanation: The gradient is the distance covered divided by the time taken, which is the speed. A flat line covers no distance, so it means standing still.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: speed = distance ÷ time
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.explanation: Slide the top intersection along a transversal onto the bottom parallel line, and tear the two base angles α, β off a triangle to place them into the exterior angle.

atlasLessons.title: Ch 14.1 · Seeing the Distribution: Histograms, Spread & Standard Deviation (Concrete Manipulation)
atlasLessons.question: How does touching the geometry of Seeing the Distribution: Histograms, Spread & Standard Deviation reveal its structure?
atlasLessons.explanation: Change the width Δx of a histogram class interval and watch the bar height adjust so its area stays equal to frequency f.
atlasLessons.limits: Formula: Frequency Density = f / Δx,   μ = (∑ xᵢ) / n,   σ = √[ (∑(xᵢ − μ)²) / n ]
stories: In a true histogram, the area of each bar — not its height — represents frequency.

atlasLessons.title: Ch 14.2 · Seeing the Distribution: Histograms, Spread & Standard Deviation (The Visual 'Aha!' Invariant)
atlasLessons.question: What stays constant in Seeing the Distribution: Histograms, Spread & Standard Deviation when you deform or slice the figure?
atlasLessons.explanation: If one class interval is twice as wide as another, keeping the bar at raw frequency makes it look twice as big by accident — dividing height by class width (Frequency Density = f / Δx) makes Area = FD × Δx = f exact!
atlasLessons.limits: Formula: Frequency Density = f / Δx,   μ = (∑ xᵢ) / n,   σ = √[ (∑(xᵢ − μ)²) / n ]

atlasLessons.title: Ch 16.2 · Updating Belief: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem (The Visual 'Aha!' Invariant)
atlasLessons.question: What stays constant in Updating Belief: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem when you deform or slice the figure?
atlasLessons.explanation: Conditioning on a positive test throws away everyone who tested negative! What remains is just two bars: 19 True Positives (red) from the 20 sick people, and 49 False Positives (amber) from the 980 healthy people — so P(D | +) = 19 / (19 + 49) ≈ 27.9%!
stories: Evidence never acts in a vacuum — it slices and renormalizes the prior base rate inside a 1,000-person unit square.

widgets.title: Two circles in a class of 30
widgets.challengePrompt: Put 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both. Predict how many students are outside both circles, then read the figure.
widgets.cutaway: 11 play cricket only, 7 play both and 8 play football only. That is 26, so 4 are outside both circles.
widgets.idealised: The rule: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Put 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The four parts are 11, 7, 8 and 4. Together they make 30.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Red is A, blue is B, the amber number is the middle, and green is outside both.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Put 22 in A and 20 in B. Why can the middle not go below 12?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two circles in your journal and write the count in each of the four parts.

widgets.title: Checking every case
widgets.challengePrompt: On paper, make a table with four rows: in A and in B, in A only, in B only, in neither. Use it to check that outside A ∪ B means outside A and outside B.
widgets.cutaway: Only the last row is outside A ∪ B. It is also the only row outside A and outside B. So (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.
widgets.idealised: The rule: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the four rows: in both, in A only, in B only, in neither.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Tick the rows that are inside A ∪ B. Three are, and one is not.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The row outside A ∪ B is the row that is outside A and outside B.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Now tick the rows outside A ∩ B. Which description picks the same three rows?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Copy the table into your journal and mark the rows for each side of the law.

widgets.title: Hunting for a counterexample
widgets.challengePrompt: Test the claim "if a number is odd, it is a multiple of 3" on the numbers 1 to 15. Find every number that breaks it.
widgets.cutaway: 1, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are odd and not multiples of 3. Any one of them breaks the claim.
widgets.idealised: One counterexample is enough to show a claim is false.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the odd numbers from 1 to 15.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Cross out each one that is a multiple of 3. Five numbers are left.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Each number left is odd and not a multiple of 3, so each one is a counterexample.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Now test "if a number is a multiple of 6, it is even". Can you break it?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: In your journal, draw the odd numbers and the multiples of 3 as two circles. Put 5 where it belongs.

widgets.title: Turning round on the number line
widgets.challengePrompt: Predict where the arrow points after 0, 1 and 2 turns. Then set the turns and check.
widgets.cutaway: Each × (−1) turns the arrow to face the other way. Its length stays the same. Two turns bring it back, so (−1) × (−1) = +1.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 1. The arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 2. The arrow faces forward again, the same length as before.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: The green arrow faces the positive numbers. The red arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: On paper, try 3 turns and then 4. Odd counts face backward. Even counts face forward.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch the number line and the two turns in your journal.

widgets.title: What two numbers share
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the two numbers to 24 and 36. Predict the HCF and the LCM, then read the bars.
widgets.cutaway: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
widgets.idealised: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the first number to 24 and the second to 36.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The blue bar shows the HCF, 12. The amber bar shows the LCM, 72.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Blue is what the two numbers share. Amber is the smallest number both divide into.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both numbers to 24. The HCF and the LCM are both 24. Can you say why?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the factor trees for 24 and 36 in your journal and circle the shared primes.

widgets.title: The doubling staircase
widgets.challengePrompt: On paper, write 2¹ to 2¹⁰ as a staircase, each step double the one before. Use it to check that 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ without multiplying it out.
widgets.cutaway: Going up one step multiplies by 2. Going up 3 steps and then 4 more is 7 steps. That is why the indices add.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 2³ is 8 and 2⁴ is 16. 8 × 16 = 128, which is the 7th step.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 3 steps and then 4 more steps make 7 steps: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Go down instead. 2⁷ ÷ 2⁴ is 4 steps down from the 7th step. Where do you land?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the staircase in your journal and mark the jump from 2³ to 2⁷.

widgets.title: Lining up the repeating digits
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the repeating digits to 36. Predict what is left when the blue row is taken from the red row. Then read the green box.
widgets.cutaway: The red row is 100 lots of 0.3636… and the blue row is 1 lot. Their digits after the point match, so they cancel. 99 lots are left, and they make 36.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the repeating digits to 36. The red row shows 36.3636… and the blue row shows 0.3636…

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: After the decimal point the two rows are identical. Taking one from the other leaves exactly 36.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Red is 100 lots of the number. Blue is 1 lot. Green is the 99 lots left over.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the repeating digits to 18. The green box gives 18/99, which is 2/11. Divide 2 by 11 on paper to check.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write the three rows for 0.3636… in your journal, with the matching digits lined up.

widgets.title: How many pieces fit?
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the whole number to 4 and the bottom of the fraction to 3. Predict how many pieces of 2/3 fit into 4. Then read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: 4 wholes cut into thirds make 12 thirds. Each piece uses 2 of them, so 6 pieces fit. That is 4 × 3 ÷ 2, which is 4 × 3/2.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the whole number to 4 and the bottom of the fraction to 3.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber line counts the pieces. 6 pieces of 2/3 fit into 4.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Multiplying by 3 counts the thirds. Dividing by 2 groups them. Together that is × 3/2.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Keep the whole number at 4 and set the bottom to 6. The pieces are smaller, so more fit. How many?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw 4 bars cut into thirds in your journal and circle the groups of 2.

widgets.title: Sharing in a ratio
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the parts for A to 2 and the parts for B to 6. Every part is worth ₹40. Predict how much A and B each get. Then read the two bars.
widgets.cutaway: Every box is 1 part and holds ₹40. A has 2 boxes and B has 6, so A gets ₹80 and B gets ₹240. Together that is 8 parts, which is ₹320.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 1 part = total ÷ number of parts

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the parts for A to 3 and the parts for B to 5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Every box is the same size and holds ₹40. A has 3 boxes and B has 5.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: There are 3 + 5 = 8 parts and ₹320 in all. ₹320 ÷ 8 = ₹40 for one part.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set A to 6 and B to 2. The total is still ₹320. Who gets more now, and how much?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two bars for 3 : 5 in your journal and write ₹40 in every box.

widgets.title: Adding or multiplying, for 20 years
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the interest rate to 10%. Predict what ₹1,000 becomes in 20 years with simple interest. Then guess the compound total, and read the amber lines.
widgets.cutaway: Simple interest adds the same ₹100 every year, so 20 years add ₹2,000. Compound interest multiplies by 1.1 every year. Twenty multiplications turn ₹1,000 into ₹6,727.
widgets.idealised: The rule: multiply by the same number once for each year

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the interest rate to 8%. The amber lines show ₹2,600 with simple interest and ₹4,661 with compound.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Compound interest gives ₹2,061 more, from the same ₹1,000 and the same rate.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Simple interest adds 20 lots of ₹80. Compound interest multiplies by 1.08 twenty times.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the rate to 12%. The rule of 72 says the money doubles every 6 years. Is the compound total more than ₹8,000?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Copy the first three years at 8% into your journal: ₹1,080, ₹1,166.40 and ₹1,259.71.

widgets.title: Two brackets as a rectangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the side to 5, the first number to 2 and the second number to 3. Predict the area of each of the four pieces. Then read the rectangle.
widgets.cutaway: The red square is 5 by 5, so it holds 25. The blue strips hold 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 5 = 15. The amber corner holds 2 × 3 = 6. Together that is 56, and 7 × 8 = 56.
widgets.idealised: The rule: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 4, the first number to 3 and the second number to 2.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red square is x², the blue strips are 3x and 2x, and the amber corner is 6.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 3x and 2x are like terms, so they join to make 5x. The green line reads x² + 5x + 6.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both numbers to 3. The two strips are the same size now. What is (x + 3)² multiplied out?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the rectangle for (x + 2)(x + 1) in your journal and write the area in each piece.

widgets.title: A square with a corner cut away
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the side to 6 and the first number to 2. Predict 6² − 2² before you read the amber lines.
widgets.cutaway: 6² − 2² = 36 − 4 = 32. The amber lines show the same number as 4 × 8, which is (6 − 2) × (6 + 2).
widgets.idealised: The rule: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 5 and the first number to 3. The amber lines show 5² − 3².

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 25 − 9 = 16, and the amber lines give 2 × 8, which is also 16.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 2 is the side take away 3, and 8 is the side add 3. So 5² − 3² = (5 − 3)(5 + 3).

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 3 and the first number to 3. Predict the answer, and say why.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a 5 by 5 square, cut a 3 by 3 corner from it, and lay the rest out as a 2 by 8 rectangle.

widgets.title: A balance for an equation
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the bags to 5 and the loose marbles to 4. Predict how many marbles a bag must hold for the right pan to show 19. Then move the last slider.
widgets.cutaway: 5 bags and 4 marbles balance 19 marbles. Take 4 off both pans, and 5 bags balance 15. So each bag holds 3.
widgets.idealised: The rule: ax + b = c gives x = (c − b) ÷ a

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the bags to 2, the loose marbles to 1 and the marbles in a bag to 4.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The right pan shows 9 marbles, and the green line reads 2b + 1 = 9.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Take 1 off both pans: 2b = 8. Share between 2 bags: b = 4, the slider's value.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the loose marbles to 9. What does the right pan show now, and why does b stay 4?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the balance for 3b + 2 = 14 in your journal. Cross out the same marbles on both pans.

widgets.title: Turning a formula round
widgets.challengePrompt: The taxi formula is C = 50 + 12d. Predict the distance for a fare of ₹110 before you work it out.
widgets.cutaway: Undo the steps in reverse order. 110 − 50 = 60, and 60 ÷ 12 = 5, so the ride was 5 km.
widgets.idealised: The rule: C = 50 + 12d gives d = (C − 50) ÷ 12

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the taxi formula as a chain: d, then × 12, then + 50, then C.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Each arrow has an inverse. Adding 50 is undone by taking 50 away, and × 12 by ÷ 12.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Run the chain backwards from C, and you get d = (C − 50) ÷ 12.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Make r the subject of A = 3r + 7. Then find r when A = 25.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the chain for v = u + at forwards and backwards, and read off t.

widgets.title: Turning an inequality round
widgets.challengePrompt: Mark 2 and 5 on a number line. Predict what happens to their order when you multiply both by −1.
widgets.cutaway: 2 < 5, but −2 > −5. Multiplying by −1 reflects every number across 0, so the order turns round.
widgets.idealised: The rule: if a < b, then −a > −b

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a number line from −6 to 6, and mark 2 and 5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Multiply each by −1. The points −2 and −5 sit on the other side of 0, the other way round.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: So 2 < 5 becomes −2 > −5. Dividing by a negative number turns the order round too.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Solve −3x < 12. Which way does the sign point once you divide by −3?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw x ≥ −1 and x < 4 on one number line, with a filled dot and an open circle.

widgets.title: Two staircases make a rectangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the terms to 6, the first term to 1 and the common difference to 1. Predict 1 + 2 + … + 6 before you read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: The red staircase 1 to 6 and its blue copy turned upside down make a rectangle 6 wide and 7 high. That is 42 squares, so one staircase is 21.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) ÷ 2

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the terms to 4, the first term to 1 and the common difference to 1.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Every column, red and blue together, is 5 high.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The rectangle is 4 × 5 = 20, and half of it is 10, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the first term to 3 and the common difference to 2. Are the columns still all the same height?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two staircases for 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 in your journal and find the sum.

widgets.title: Finding the rule from the gaps
widgets.challengePrompt: Write down 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. Predict whether its first differences or its second differences are equal.
widgets.cutaway: The first differences are 4, 6, 8 and 10. The second differences are all 2, so the nth term starts with n².
widgets.idealised: The rule: equal first differences d give dn + c, and equal second differences 2a give an² + …

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and the gaps under it.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The gaps are all 4, so the nth term starts with 4n.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 4n gives 4, 8, 12, so take 1 away: the nth term is 4n − 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Try 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. The first gaps change, so find the gaps of the gaps.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the tile squares for 1, 4 and 9, and colour each new L-shaped border.

widgets.title: Rise over run stays the same
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the gradient to 3 and where the line crosses the y-axis to −2. Predict where it crosses the x-axis before you read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: y = 3x − 2 crosses the y-axis at (0, −2). Setting y = 0 gives 3x = 2, so it crosses the x-axis at x = 2 ÷ 3.
widgets.idealised: The rule: y = mx + c, with gradient m = change in y ÷ change in x

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to 1, where the line crosses the y-axis to 0 and the step across to 1.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Change the step across to 3. The rise becomes 3 too, so the gradient is still 1.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to −1. The line now falls 1 for every 1 across.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to 0. Where does the flat line cross the x-axis?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 on the same axes in your journal. Do they meet?

widgets.title: Reading a journey
widgets.challengePrompt: Kym rides 12 km in 1 hour, rests for 1 hour, then rides home in 2 hours. Predict which part of the line is steepest.
widgets.cutaway: The ride out climbs 12 in 1 hour, so its gradient is 12. The ride home falls 12 in 2 hours, a gradient of −6.
widgets.idealised: The rule: on a distance-time graph, speed = distance ÷ time = the gradient

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Mark the points (0, 0), (1, 12), (2, 12) and (4, 0), and join them.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The flat part is the rest stop. Time passes, but the distance does not change.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The first part rises 12 in 1 hour, which is a speed of 12 km an hour.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: If the ride home took 3 hours, would its line be steeper or less steep?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the line of your own trip to school and back, and find each speed.

widgets.title: Parallel Transversal Proof
widgets.challengePrompt: Manipulate Parallel Transversal Proof until the visual invariant locks in, then verify θ_ext = α + β,   ∑ interior angles of n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°,   M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
widgets.cutaway: Intuition → Formula Lockstep: Because a parallel translation changes no angles, α and β fit flush inside the exterior angle next to γ — proving both α + β + γ = 180° and ext = α + β at once!
widgets.idealised: Formula Anatomy: θ_ext = α + β,   ∑ interior angles of n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°,   M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2)

watchSteps.title: 1. Concrete Touch
watchSteps.caption: Slide the top intersection along a transversal onto the bottom parallel line, and tear the two base angles α, β off a triangle to place them into the exterior angle.

watchSteps.title: 2. Spot the Invariant ('Aha!')
watchSteps.caption: Because a parallel translation changes no angles, α and β fit flush inside the exterior angle next to γ — proving both α + β + γ = 180° and ext = α + β at once!

watchSteps.title: 3. Colour-Map the Symbols
watchSteps.caption: Match red, blue, amber, and green geometry to θ_ext = α + β,   ∑ interior angles of n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°,   M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

watchSteps.title: 4. Test a Boundary Case
watchSteps.caption: Push the slider to 0, 1, or 90° and verify that the formula predicts the exact extreme state.

watchSteps.title: 5. Stamp & Sketch in Journal
watchSteps.caption: Freeze the state into your Cornell Proof & Construction Journal.

widgets.title: Exterior Angle Tear Proof
widgets.challengePrompt: Manipulate Exterior Angle Tear Proof until the visual invariant locks in, then verify θ_ext = α + β,   ∑ interior angles of n-gon = (n − 2) × 180°,   M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
widgets.cutaway: Intuition → Formula Lockstep: Because a parallel translation changes no angles, α and β fit flush inside the exterior angle next to γ — proving both α + β + γ = 180° and ext = α + β at once!

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 3 · Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio (6L² vs L³)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why Elephants Have Huge Ears & Cells Stay Microscopic (SA:V Scaling)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: When a cell or organism enlarges by linear scale factor k, its surface area grows as k² while its metabolising volume grows as k³ — so SA/V = 6/L drops inversely with size.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: SA = 6L²,   V = L³   ⇒   SA : V = 6 / L
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: If a cubical cell doubles its side length from L = 1 μm to L = 2 μm (k = 2), by what factor does its Surface-Area-to-Volume ratio change?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Surface area multiplies by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so SA:V halves from 6:1 to 3:1.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 13 · Mendel's Punnett Squares & Clinical Screening
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Punnett Grids Are 2×2 Area Diagrams & Medical Tests Obey Bayes' Rule
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A Punnett square for Aa × Aa is literally the algebraic expansion (0.5A + 0.5a)² = 0.25AA + 0.50Aa + 0.25aa, and genetic carrier screening relies on Bayes' theorem.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: In a cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), given that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype (AA or Aa), what is the conditional probability it is a carrier (Aa)?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Out of 3 dominant-phenotype boxes (1 AA and 2 Aa), 2 are Aa, so P(Aa | Dominant) = 2/3.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Physics Ch 1 · Kinematics (Velocity Slope & Displacement Area)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Velocity Is the Derivative of Position; Displacement Is the Area Under v(t)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: On a distance-time graph, gradient Δs/Δt is speed. On a speed-time graph, the area of the trapezium under v(t) is distance travelled s = v₀t + ½at².
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: v(t) = ds/dt,   Δs = ∫ v(t) dt = v₀t + ½at²
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: A train accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over 8 seconds. Using the trapezium area under v(t), how far does it travel?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Physics Ch 2 · Newton's Laws & Inclined Planes
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Resolving Forces on a Ramp with Unit-Circle Sine & Cosine Shadows
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A block of weight mg on a ramp of angle θ splits into a component mg sin θ pulling down the slope and mg cos θ pressing into the ramp.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: F_parallel = mg sin θ,   F_normal = mg cos θ
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: For a 100 N crate on a 30° ramp, what component of gravity pulls it down the slope?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Chemistry · Balancing Equations as Linear Conservation & Mole Ratios
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Chemical Stoichiometry Is Ratio Partition & First-Order Kinetics Is dy/dt = −ky
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Balancing a reaction solves a system of linear conservation equations for atoms, and radioactive/chemical decay follows the exponential differential equation dy/dt = −ky.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: If a sample of 80 g decays with a half-life of 3 hours, how much remains after 9 hours?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Economics Fig E.1 · ₹1,000 a Month at 8% Compounding Machine
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why Starting Early Beats Saving Twice as Much Later (The Geometric Series of Wealth)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Saving ₹1,000 a month at 8% for 20 years puts ₹2.40 lakh in, which compounds to ₹5.89 lakh — more than half of the final pot is interest earned on interest.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: A = P(1 + r)ⁿ,   Rule of 72: Doubling Years ≈ 72 / (Rate %)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: Using the Rule of 72, approximately how many years does it take a lump sum to double at 8% annual compound interest?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Mathematics Ch 5 · Fourier Epicycles & Musical Harmonics
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why a Violin and a Flute Playing the Same Note Sound Different (Fourier Series)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Pythagoras discovered that string ratios 1:2 (octave) and 2:3 (fifth) make consonance; Fourier proved any periodic sound wave is a sum of spinning unit-circle harmonics bₙ sin(nt).
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: f(t) = (4/π)(sin t + ⅓ sin 3t + ⅕ sin 5t + …)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: In the square-wave Fourier series, what is the amplitude ratio of the 3rd harmonic (sin 3t) to the fundamental (sin t)?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Mathematics · 2×2 Matrix Graphics & Boolean Logic Gates
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: How iPad GPUs Rotate 3D Worlds with Matrices & CPUs Think with De Morgan Gates
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Every pixel and 3D vertex on Kym's iPad is rotated and projected by matrix multiplication, while every CPU transistor evaluates Boolean logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND).
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: R_θ = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]],   ¬(P ∧ Q) ⇔ (¬P) ∨ (¬Q)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: What is the determinant det(R_θ) of a 2D rotation matrix through any angle θ?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: det(R_θ) = cos²θ − (−sin²θ) = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 (rotation preserves area).

topics.title: Expressions, formulae and equations
topics.summary: An expression has no = sign, such as 3x + 2. An equation is true for only some values of x, such as 3x + 2 = 11. An identity is true for every value, such as 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw the bar model or a sketch before you write the formula for 2.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Expanding brackets
topics.summary: A number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside, signs included: −3(x − 5) = −3x + 15. For two brackets, multiply each term of one by each term of the other, then collect like terms.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw the bar model or a sketch before you write the formula for 2.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Factorizing expressions
topics.summary: Take the HCF of every term outside a bracket, numbers and letters both: 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Then check that nothing common is left inside. A difference of two squares factorises as (a − b)(a + b).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw the bar model or a sketch before you write the formula for 2.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Substitution into expressions
topics.summary: Put each number in a bracket as you substitute it. When x = −4, x² is (−4)² = 16, but −x² is −16. Work out powers before you multiply.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 72 and 120 using prime factorisation, and verify that HCF × LCM = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1 (Prime Factor Trees): 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3¹ × 5¹.
Step 2 (Venn Intersection = HCF): Take min powers: 2³ × 3¹ = 24.
Step 3 (Venn Union = LCM): Take max powers: 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360.
Step 4 (Invariant Check): 24 × 360 = 8640 = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: HCF = 24 and LCM = 360 because 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; their overlap is 2³ × 3 = 24 and their union is 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Expand and simplify 4(2x − 3) − 3(x − 5), and explain using the area/number-line model why the constant term becomes +3.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Factorise completely: 18a²b − 12ab².
schoolQuestions.workedExample:

polyaStages.title: 1. Understand the Problem
polyaStages.subtitle: Name what you want, what you're given, and the smaller questions hiding inside
prompts: What am I trying to find? Can I name it, or draw it as a bar?
What facts am I given, and what stays the same? Look for facts hiding in words like 'constant', 'bisects' or 'regular'.
What smaller questions hide inside this one? List the pieces.
polyaStages.exampleProblem: A train passes a 300 m platform in 24 seconds and passes a standing lamp-post in 9 seconds at constant speed. Find the length of the train.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Want: the train's length L. Given: the lamp-post takes 9 s (the train's own length), the platform takes 24 s (the train plus 300 m), and the speed never changes. Pieces: the train's speed, and how long the 300 m takes on its own.

polyaStages.title: 2. Devise a Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Pick the piece you can crack right now. If none gives, change the picture: a bar model, a smaller version, working backwards, or symmetry
prompts: Which piece can I solve right now, with only what I'm given? Start there.
If no piece gives way, can I draw a bar model, or add a helper line to the figure?
Can I try a smaller version first (n = 1, 2, 3), or work backwards from what I want?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Put the train's two journeys on one bar and look for a piece you can solve.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Piece found: the extra 300 m. Bar 1 is [train] and takes 9 s. Bar 2 is [train] + [300 m] and takes 24 s. So the 300 m on its own takes 24 − 9 = 15 s. We can crack that now: it's the foothold.

polyaStages.title: 3. Carry Out the Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Crack the foothold, then use its answer to open the next piece, until the whole problem gives
prompts: What did my first piece give me, and which piece does it open next?
Does each step follow from the line above it?
Are my units and signs still right? Can I say what each middle number means?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Use the 15-second piece to find the speed, then the speed to find L.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Piece solved: 300 m in 15 s, so the speed is 300 ÷ 15 = 20 m/s. Piece used: the lamp-post takes 9 s at 20 m/s. Whole solved: L = 20 × 9 = 180 m.

polyaStages.title: 4. Look Back & Generalise
polyaStages.subtitle: Check the answer, check the pieces fit back together, and keep the move for next time
prompts: Does the answer work in the original problem?
Did my pieces fit back together? Which piece was the key one, and how did I spot it?
Can I write a rule for any platform length P and times t₁ and t₂?
Where else could 'compare two cases and subtract' find me a foothold?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Check L = 180 m, name the key piece, and write the rule.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Check: (180 + 300) ÷ 20 = 24 s ✓. Key piece: the extra 300 m, found by comparing the two journeys. Rule: L = P · t₁ ÷ (t₂ − t₁).

visualMathTips.title: Why minus times minus is plus
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Multiplying by −1 turns you round on the number line.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Two about-turns leave you facing the way you started.

visualMathTips.title: Why (a + b)² is not a² + b²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Draw a square of side a + b. Mark a and b along the top and down the side, and cut it into four pieces.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: There are the corner squares a² and b², and also two strips of area ab. Leave out the 2ab and the square has two gaps.

visualMathTips.title: Why 1 + 2 + … + n is half of n(n + 1)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Build a staircase of 1, 2, 3, … up to n blocks. Make a copy and turn it upside down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Set the copy on top, and every column reaches n + 1. The two staircases fill a rectangle n by n + 1, so one staircase is half of it.

visualMathTips.title: Why a Circle's Area Is πr²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Slice a circle into 24 pizza sectors and comb them together alternating up and down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The wavy top and bottom each use half the circumference (πr), while the height is the radius r — forming a rectangle of base πr and height r!

visualMathTips.title: Why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for Every Angle
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: On the unit circle of radius 1, level light casts vertical shadow sin θ and top light casts horizontal shadow cos θ.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Those two shadows are the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 — so their squares always add to 1² = 1!

visualMathTips.title: Why a Positive Result from a 95% Accurate Test Is Wrong 72% of the Time
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: In the 1,000-person unit square at 2% prevalence, only 20 people are sick while 980 are healthy.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: 5% false alarms on 980 healthy people creates 49 false positives (amber), dwarfing the 19 true positives (red)!

visualMathTips.title: Why Slope and Area Are Inverses (FTC)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Compare the blue triangle of area under f′(t) = t with the red height bar of f(x) = ½x².
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Each thin strip of area f′(t)·dt equals df — the tiny vertical step of the original curve. Summing all tiny rises gives total height f(x) − f(0)!

visualMathTips.title: Why det(A) = ad − bc Is Area
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Drag the red basis vector Aî = (a, c) and blue basis vector Aĵ = (b, d) in the 2×2 Matrix Sandbox.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The unit 1×1 square deforms into a parallelogram whose bounding box (a+b)(c+d), minus four right triangles and two b×c rectangles, leaves exact area ad − bc!
